prime.problem: A tree only approaches the price, with an error that shrinks like 1/N, and it gives the hedge only node by node. A desk re-pricing thousands of options a second needs an exact price and exact sensitivities, so it knows how many shares to hold and how that hedge will drift.
prime.fits: Second card of the pricing part. It is the binomial tree's continuous limit, running on the GBM card's lognormal model with μ replaced by r. Delta and gamma are the option's versions of the bond card's duration and convexity.
prime.goal: Compute the shared call and put by hand, check parity, read each Greek as a hedge instruction, and explain why a delta-hedged short option loses on big moves.

attend: What do the two terms of the call formula correspond to in the replicating portfolio?
Why does put–call parity hold for any model, and what does that make it useful for?
Why is delta both a slope and a number of shares?
How does gamma explain the hedged book's loss on a move to 105?
Why does the finite-difference gamma blow up at h = 10<sup>−7</sup>?

must: GBM + continuous, costless hedging → a changing mix of shares and cash copies a European payoff exactly → the price is the copy's cost → C = S₀N(d₁) (shares held, in $) − Ke<sup>−rT</sup>N(d₂) (cash borrowed)

A call minus a put with the same K and T pays S<sub>T</sub> − K in every state → that's a forward, worth S − Ke<sup>−rT</sup> today → C − P = 4.8771 whatever the model → a free check on any pricing code

Delta = ∂C/∂S = N(d₁) → hold 0.6368 shares per short call to be flat to small moves → but the price curve bends (gamma 0.0188) → big moves either way lose against the hedge (−0.2231 at 105) → re-hedge often, and the short option collects theta in exchange

Price convex in S and increasing in σ → more volatility raises the option's value (vega 0.3752 per vol point) → σ is the only input you can't look up → the market quotes σ (implied vol) and uses the formula as a translator
elevated: Bump-and-reprice Greeks need a step h that balances truncation error against floating-point rounding → at h = 10<sup>−7</sup> the second difference divides rounding noise by 10<sup>−14</sup> → gamma comes out −0.71 instead of 0.0188 → closed forms (or adjoint methods) avoid this
reference: the PDE check θ + ½σ²S²Γ + rSΔ = rC

compress.prompt: Write the call formula from memory and label each term as a position in the replicating portfolio. Then draw the call price against S with the tangent at 100 and mark what delta and gamma are on the picture.
checklist: shares term S₀N(d₁), borrowed-cash term Ke<sup>−rT</sup>N(d₂)
parity C − P = S − Ke<sup>−rT</sup> holds for any model
delta = slope = hedge ratio; gamma = curvature = hedge drift
N(d₂) is the risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money, not the real one

retrieve.q: Explain what a market maker who sold the shared call does to be hedged, and why they must keep trading afterwards.
answer: buy N(d₁) = 0.6368 shares, financed by borrowing about 53.23
as S moves, delta changes at rate gamma (0.0188 per $1)
so the hedge goes stale and must be rebalanced; big moves between rebalances lose money (short gamma)

retrieve.q: Walk through d₁, d₂ and the call price for S = 90, K = 100, r = 5%, σ = 20%, T = 1.
You need delta and vega for 10,000 options in a model with no closed form. Compare bump-and-reprice with the analytic formulas you have here: cost, accuracy, and how each can fail.
answer: bumping: 2–3 extra prices per Greek per option, works in any model
it depends on h: too big and it measures the bend, too small and rounding error swamps it (gamma −0.71 at h = 10<sup>−7</sup>)
closed forms here are exact and O(1), but exist only for this model; adjoint (AAD) methods get all Greeks for a few times one price

compare.q: The tree's Δ at one node and Black–Scholes delta N(d₁): how are they the same object, and why does the tree converge to the formula only like 1/N?
answer: both are the shares that make the portfolio riskless over the next instant or step
as Δt → 0, the tree's per-step hedge becomes the continuous hedge
the error is 1/N because the terminal distribution and the kink at K are sampled on a grid, which is why it zig-zags with N's parity

compare.q: Adjoint algorithmic differentiation records the pricing computation on a tape. Why does that beat bumping for Greeks, and what does it cost?
answer: one backward sweep gives the derivative with respect to every input, for a small multiple of one pricing run
bumping needs extra re-prices per input and suffers from h
the tape costs memory, proportional to the operations recorded

predict.q: Set r = 0 for the shared contract. Traders quote "ATM call ≈ 0.4 × S × σ × √T". What does the rule give, what does Black–Scholes give, and why does r = 5% push the true price up to 10.45? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: The rule gives 0.4 × 100 × 0.2 × 1 = 8.00; Black–Scholes at r = 0 gives 7.9656, very close (0.4 ≈ 1/√(2π)). With r = 5% the strike's present value falls to 95.12, so the call is effectively in the money by the forward: C rises to 10.4506. Parity says C − P = 4.8771, and that gap is all rates.

apply.task: Use the card's price() and greeks() to (1) reprice the shared call at σ = 30% and check that vega predicted the direction and rough size; (2) compute delta and gamma at T = 0.25 and compare with T = 1; (3) delta-hedge a short call at S = 100 and compute the hedged P&L if S jumps to 95.
apply.done: (1) C = 14.2313, up 3.78 against vega's linear estimate 37.52 × 0.10 = 3.75. (2) At T = 0.25: delta 0.5695, gamma 0.0393, more than double gamma at T = 1 (0.0188). (3) Hedged P&L = 0.6368 × (−5) − (C(95) − 10.4506) = −3.1842 − (7.5109 − 10.4506) = −0.2444: short gamma loses on a drop too, about as much as on the rise to 105 (−0.2231).
apply.hint: For (3), compute C(95) with price(95, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1) and remember you are short the call and long 0.6368 shares.
